summary:
Fiji decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct under the Crimes Act 2010, in force from 1 February 2010, repealing a colonial-era offence that had carried up to fourteen years' imprisonment. Arrests had already ceased in 2006, when the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.

The 2013 Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression alongside sexual orientation. The Asia Pacific Alliance describes that pairing as unique worldwide, and its 2023 policy brief treats it as the central legal fact for trans people in Fiji. Fiji was, with South Africa, one of the first two countries to enshrine sexual-orientation non-discrimination in a constitution, in 1997; the 2013 text reinstated and expanded that protection.

The constitutional guarantee has no implementing machinery for trans people. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, and the Asia Pacific Alliance records the resulting marginalisation and discrimination as documented. The traditional third-gender role known as vaka sa lewa lewa holds cultural recognition only, with no legal standing.

There is no route to recognition of a same-sex partner: the Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as one man and one woman, and no civil union exists. Health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation, while intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected in law.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement history is recent and well documented. In April 2005 two men, one of them an Australian tourist, received two-year prison sentences under Penal Code Article 175; the sentencing judge called the acts "so disgusting ... any decent person vomit". Human Rights Watch demanded that the charges be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Days after those sentences, Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, describing homosexuality as a sin in "the conservative Christian nation". That political and religious climate persisted through the 2006 no-arrest policy and the 2009 abolition of the constitution, before decriminalisation in 2010.

Criminalisation was also linked to public-health harm: an executive of the NZ AIDS Foundation argued in 2006 that the offence drove sex underground and fed HIV transmission.

Fiji's constitutional sequence is unusual. Sexual-orientation protection entered the 1997 constitution, workplace protection followed in 2007, that constitution was abolished in 2009, decriminalisation came in 2010, and the 2013 constitution added gender identity and expression to the protected grounds.
localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since 2007.

Health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation.

Outright International's country overview reports that organisations cannot register, a constraint on organised LGBT advocacy and service provision.

The traditional third-gender role of vaka sa lewa lewa is recognised in Fijian culture but confers no legal status, and legislative frameworks do not recognise third-gender identities for any official purpose.

Intersex bodily autonomy is not protected in law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's overview carries an "at a glance" flag marking same-sex relations as illegal, which contradicts the same overview's account of decriminalisation under the Crimes Act 2010. The inventory does not explain the flag; the inconsistency is unresolved, and the 2010 repeal is corroborated by the other sources listed here.

The GlobalGayz country page is undated and pre-dates the 2013 constitution. Its statement that sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination is not banned describes the earlier legal position, not current law.

No source in the inventory quantifies violence or harassment against trans people in Fiji, and none reports a decided case testing the 2013 constitution's gender-identity and expression clause. Enforcement of that protection is not documented here.

The report that LGBT organisations cannot register rests on a summary flag in one overview, without detail on the registration regime or which organisations are affected.
